title: History, culture and identity
objectives: I can read and discuss short texts about the history of Ukraine, from Kyivan Rus and the Cossacks to the independence of 1991.
I can tell past events in the historical present, using imperfective verbs such as 'очо́лює' and 'проголо́шує' for single completed events.
I can place an event in time in historical writing: in a part of a century, from one century to another, for a span of centuries and before our era.
I can sort any noun into the four declensions of Ukrainian grammar and use its declension to predict its endings.
I can talk about Christmas, Easter and other traditions, give the holiday greetings, and discuss language and identity.

vocabulary.note: Both the past of a country or a people and a story that someone tells: 'Це до́вга істо́рія.', 'It's a long story.' Its genitive and dative are 'істо́рії', and its instrumental is 'істо́рією'. The adjective is 'істори́чний', historical, with the stress on 'ри'.

example.source: Sam is very interested in the history of Ukraine.

vocabulary.note: Made from 'незале́жний', independent, with the suffix '-ість'. The 'і' of the suffix becomes 'о' before the ending '-і', as in the genitive 'незале́жності'; the instrumental 'незале́жністю' keeps 'і'. 'День Незале́жності', Independence Day, is August 24, and both words of its name begin with a capital letter.

example.target: Два́дцять четве́ртого се́рпня Украї́на святку́є День Незале́жності.
example.source: On August 24 Ukraine celebrates Independence Day.
example.source_literal: Twenty of-fourth of-August Ukraine celebrates Day of-Independence.

vocabulary.note: The country as a political body, with its government and its laws. 'Краї́на' is the country as a land and its people. The adjective is 'держа́вний': 'держа́вна мо́ва', the state language.

example.source: Kyivan Rus was a large state.

vocabulary.note: The everyday and legal word: 'свобо́да сло́ва', freedom of speech. 'Во́ля' also means freedom, and also will; it is the word of poetry and of older texts. The adjective for a free person or people is 'ві́льний'.

example.source: The Cossacks loved freedom.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'козака́', plural 'козаки́', 'козакі́в': the stress moves to the ending. The adjective is 'коза́цький', and the vocative is 'коза́че'. The word is written with a small letter.

example.source: Taras is reading a book about the Cossacks.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'гетьма́на'. The hetman was the elected head of the Cossack army and, from 1648, of the Cossack state, 'Гетьма́нщина', the Hetmanate. The title is written with a small letter: 'гетьма́н Богда́н Хмельни́цький'.

example.source: Bohdan Khmelnytsky was a hetman.

vocabulary.note: The plural of 'пре́док', an ancestor, which loses its 'о' when an ending is added: 'пре́дка', 'пре́дки', 'пре́дків'. The plural is the form in everyday use.

example.source: We remember our ancestors.

vocabulary.note: What a people, a family or a person receives from earlier generations: songs, customs, a house, a language. 'Культу́рна спа́дщина' is cultural heritage.

example.target: Ці пісні́ співа́ли ще на́ші пре́дки. Це на́ша спа́дщина.
example.source: Our ancestors already sang these songs. They are our heritage.
example.source_literal: These songs sang already our ancestors. This our heritage.

vocabulary.note: Both the ability to remember and what a people remembers: 'па́м’ять про війну́', the memory of the war. A single recollection is 'спо́гад'. Genitive 'па́м’яті', instrumental 'па́м’яттю'. It shares its root with 'пам’ята́ти', to remember, and 'пам’я́тник', monument.

example.source: Grandma has a good memory.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'війни́', plural 'ві́йни', with the stress moving to the stem in the plural. 'Під час війни́' means during the war.

example.target: Під час війни́ це мі́сто зруйнува́ли.
example.source: The town was destroyed during the war.

vocabulary.note: Made from 'іденти́чний', identical, with the suffix '-ість', like 'незале́жність'; genitive 'іденти́чності'. It names who a person or a people feels they are: 'украї́нська іденти́чність'.

example.source: The language became part of her identity.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'тради́ції', plural 'тради́ції'. 'За тради́цією' means by tradition, and the adjective is 'тради́ційний'.

example.target: У на́шій сім’ї́ є тради́ція: на Різдво́ ми співа́ємо коля́дки.
example.source: Our family has a tradition: at Christmas we sing carols.
example.source_literal: In our family is tradition: on Christmas we sing carols.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'звича́ю', plural 'звича́ї'. A custom belongs to a community; one person's habit is 'зви́чка'. 'За звича́єм' means by custom.

example.source: This is an old Ukrainian custom.

vocabulary.note: From 'вишива́ти', to embroider. Every region has its own patterns and colors. Its locative is 'у вишива́нці', with 'к' becoming 'ц' before '-і'.

example.target: Сем купи́в собі́ вишива́нку у Льво́ві.
example.source: Sam bought himself an embroidered shirt in Lviv.
example.source_literal: Sam bought to-self embroidered-shirt in Lviv.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'рушника́', plural 'рушники́'. The word names any towel. An embroidered one is used at weddings and holidays and to welcome guests, and it hangs above icons and family photos.

example.target: Госте́й зустріча́ють хлі́бом і сі́ллю на рушнику́.
example.source: Guests are welcomed with bread and salt on an embroidered towel.
example.source_literal: Guests they-meet by-bread and by-salt on towel.

vocabulary.note: From 'писа́ти', to write, because its pattern is drawn on the egg in wax before the egg goes into the dye. An egg dyed in one color is 'кра́шанка'.

example.source: Before Easter, Grandma makes decorated Easter eggs.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'Різдва́'. 'На Різдво́', with the accusative, means for Christmas or at Christmas, and 'З Різдво́м!' is the greeting 'Merry Christmas!'. Since 2023 Ukraine has celebrated it on December 25.

example.target: На Різдво́ ми ї́демо до бабу́сі.
example.source: We're going to Grandma's for Christmas.
example.source_literal: On Christmas we go to grandma.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'Вели́кодня', with the 'е' of 'день' dropped and 'о' between the two parts. 'На Вели́кдень' means at Easter, and 'З Вели́коднем!' is the greeting 'Happy Easter!'. Its date changes every year.

example.target: Цього́ ро́ку Вели́кдень бу́де в кві́тні.
example.source: This year Easter will be in April.
example.source_literal: Of-this of-year Easter will-be in April.

vocabulary.note: From 'коля́да', the old winter festival. Going from house to house to sing carols is 'колядува́ти' ('коляду́ю', 'коляду́єш'), and the singers are 'коля́дники'. A song for New Year's Eve is 'щедрі́вка'.

example.source: This carol is very old.

vocabulary.note: '-ува-' becomes '-у-' in the present: 'святку́ю', 'святку́єш', 'святку́ють'. Its perfective is 'відсвяткува́ти'. It is built on 'свя́то', holiday.

example.target: Ми завжди́ святку́ємо Різдво́ в батькі́в.
example.source: We always celebrate Christmas at my parents'.
example.source_literal: We always celebrate Christmas at parents.

dialogues.title: Christmas Eve at Halyna's table
dialogues.context: It is December 24, Christmas Eve, 'Святве́чір', and Sam is a guest at the home of Oksana's parents, Halyna and Mykola. Sam says 'ви' to Halyna and Mykola, and they say 'ти' to him and to Oksana. 'Не́бо' is the sky, 'зі́рка' a star and 'стра́ва' a dish. 'Кутя́' is a dish of boiled wheat with poppy seeds, honey and nuts. 'Сіда́ти за стіл', literally 'to-sit behind table', is to sit down at the table, and 'з’яви́тися' is to appear. 'Що це за...?', literally 'what this for...?', asks what kind of thing something is. 'Стіна́' is a wall, 'берегти́' is to keep safe ('бережу́', 'бережемо́'), and 'впе́рше' means for the first time.

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Се́ме, сіда́й за стіл. Але́ вече́ряти ми почнемо́, коли́ на не́бі з’я́виться пе́рша зі́рка.
lines.source: Sam, sit down at the table. But we'll start dinner when the first star appears in the sky.
lines.source_literal: Sam, sit behind table. But to-have-dinner we will-begin, when on sky will-appear first star.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Пе́рша зі́рка? А чому́ зі́рка, па́ні Гали́но?
lines.source: The first star? But why a star, Ms. Halyna?
lines.source_literal: First star? And why star, Ms. Halyna?

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: За тради́цією, вона́ нага́дує про ту зі́рку, яку́ лю́ди поба́чили, коли́ народи́вся Христо́с.
lines.source: By tradition, it recalls the star that people saw when Christ was born.
lines.source_literal: By tradition, it reminds about that star, which people saw, when was-born Christ.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Ма́мо, ось вона́! Над буди́нком, ба́чите?
lines.source: Mom, there it is! Above the building, do you see?
lines.source_literal: Mom, here it! Over building, you-see?

lines.speaker: Мико́ла
lines.target: Тоді́ почина́ємо. Се́ме, сього́дні в нас двана́дцять страв, і всі без м’я́са.
lines.source: Then let's begin. Sam, tonight we have twelve dishes, and all of them without meat.
lines.source_literal: Then we-begin. Sam, today at us twelve of-dishes, and all without meat.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Двана́дцять? Чому́ так бага́то?
lines.source: Twelve? Why so many?
lines.source_literal: Twelve? Why so much?

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Ка́жуть, що це двана́дцять мі́сяців ро́ку. А почина́ємо ми за звича́єм з куті́. Спро́буй.
lines.source: People say they stand for the twelve months of the year. And by custom we begin with kutia. Try some.
lines.source_literal: They-say, that this twelve months of-year. And begin we by custom from kutia. Try.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ду́же смачно́! А що це за рушни́к на стіні́?
lines.source: Very tasty! And what is that embroidered towel on the wall?
lines.source_literal: Very tasty! And what this for towel on wall?

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Його́ вишива́ла моя́ бабу́ся. Цьому́ рушнику́ вже сто ро́ків.
lines.source: My grandmother embroidered it. This towel is already a hundred years old.
lines.source_literal: It embroidered my grandmother. To-this towel already hundred of-years.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Для на́шої сім’ї́ це спа́дщина. Ми бережемо́ його́ для свят.
lines.source: For our family it's an heirloom. We keep it for holidays.
lines.source_literal: For our family this heritage. We keep it for holidays.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А коля́дки ви сього́дні співа́тимете?
lines.source: And will you sing carols tonight?
lines.source_literal: And carols you today will-sing?

lines.speaker: Мико́ла
lines.target: Обов’язко́во, пі́сля вече́рі. А в Кана́ді на Різдво́ коляду́ють?
lines.source: Definitely, after dinner. And do people go caroling at Christmas in Canada?
lines.source_literal: Definitely, after dinner. And in Canada on Christmas they-carol?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: У Кана́ді живе́ бага́то украї́нців, і вони́ теж коляду́ють. Але́ таку́ вече́рю я ба́чу впе́рше.
lines.source: Many Ukrainians live in Canada, and they go caroling too. But this is the first time I've seen a dinner like this.
lines.source_literal: In Canada lives many of-Ukrainians, and they also carol. But such dinner I see for-the-first-time.

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Тоді́ смачно́ї куті́, Се́ме! І з Різдво́м!
lines.source: Then enjoy your kutia, Sam! And Merry Christmas!
lines.source_literal: Then of-tasty of-kutia, Sam! And with Christmas!

dialogues.title: An exhibition about the Cossacks
dialogues.context: Taras is in Kyiv for the weekend, and he and Sam visit an exhibition, 'ви́ставка', about the Cossacks at a history museum. Bohdan, a guide, shows them around; he says 'ви' to the visitors, and Sam and Taras say 'ти' to each other. 'Хто такі́...?', literally 'who such...?', asks who certain people are. 'Пі́вдень' is the south, 'назива́ти' is to call or to name, and 'чужи́й' means foreign. 'Поро́ги' are the rapids that once blocked the Dnipro, 'Дніпро́', and 'Січ', the Sich, was a fortified camp of the Cossacks; 'Запоро́зька Січ', the Zaporozhian Sich, was the one beyond the rapids. 'Засно́вувати' is to found, and 'форте́ця' is a fortress. 'Обира́ти' is to elect, and 'булава́' is a mace, the hetman's 'знак вла́ди', sign of authority. 'Істо́рики' are historians and 'екскурсово́ди' tour guides. 'Ні́би' means as if, 'відбува́тися' is to take place, and 'на на́ших оча́х', literally 'on our eyes', means before our eyes. 'Гімн' is the national anthem, and 'недарма́' means not without reason. 'Портре́т' is a portrait. 'Мину́ле', the past, is a noun that declines like the adjective 'мину́лий', last or past.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: До́брий день! Ця ви́ставка розповіда́є про украї́нських козакі́в.
lines.source: Good afternoon! This exhibition tells the story of the Ukrainian Cossacks.
lines.source_literal: Good day! This exhibition tells about Ukrainian Cossacks.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: До́брий день. Я ча́сто чу́ю сло́во «коза́к», але́ хто такі́ козаки́?
lines.source: Good afternoon. I often hear the word 'Cossack', but who were the Cossacks?
lines.source_literal: Good day. I often hear word 'Cossack', but who such Cossacks?

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: У п’ятна́дцятому столі́тті на пі́вдні Украї́ни з’явля́ються ві́льні лю́ди, які́ не хо́чуть жи́ти під чужо́ю вла́дою.
lines.source: In the fifteenth century free people appear in the south of Ukraine who do not want to live under foreign rule.
lines.source_literal: In fifteenth century on south of-Ukraine appear free people, who not want to-live under foreign authority.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Їх назива́ють козака́ми. Ка́жуть, що сло́во «коза́к» означа́є «ві́льна люди́на».
lines.source: They're called Cossacks. People say the word 'Cossack' means 'a free person'.
lines.source_literal: Them they-call by-Cossacks. They-say, that word 'Cossack' means 'free person'.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А де вони́ жили́?
lines.source: And where did they live?

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: За поро́гами Дніпра́. У шістна́дцятому столі́тті вони́ засно́вують там Запоро́зьку Січ, свою́ форте́цю.
lines.source: Beyond the Dnipro rapids. In the sixteenth century they found the Zaporozhian Sich there, their fortress.
lines.source_literal: Behind rapids of-Dnipro. In sixteenth century they found there Zaporozhian Sich, own fortress.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А хто очо́лював козакі́в?
lines.source: And who led the Cossacks?

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Гетьма́н. Його́ обира́ють самі́ козаки́. Ось його́ булава́, знак вла́ди.
lines.source: The hetman. The Cossacks elect him themselves. Here is his mace, the sign of his authority.
lines.source_literal: Hetman. Him elect themselves Cossacks. Here his mace, sign of-authority.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: А це портре́т Богда́на Хмельни́цького. Се́ме, ти чув про ньо́го?
lines.source: And this is a portrait of Bohdan Khmelnytsky. Sam, have you heard of him?
lines.source_literal: And this portrait of-Bohdan of-Khmelnytsky. Sam, you heard about him?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Чув. Він очо́лив повста́ння в сімна́дцятому столі́тті, пра́вда?
lines.source: I have. He led an uprising in the seventeenth century, didn't he?
lines.source_literal: Heard. He led uprising in seventeenth century, truth?

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Так. У ти́сяча шістсо́т со́рок восьмо́му ро́ці почина́ється повста́ння, і незаба́ром виника́є коза́цька держа́ва.
lines.source: Yes. In 1648 the uprising begins, and soon a Cossack state comes into being.
lines.source_literal: Yes. In thousand six-hundred forty eighth year begins uprising, and soon arises Cossack state.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Чому́ ви розповіда́єте про мину́ле в тепе́рішньому ча́сі?
lines.source: Why are you telling us about the past in the present tense?
lines.source_literal: Why you tell about past in present tense?

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Так розповіда́ють істо́рики й екскурсово́ди: мину́ле ні́би відбува́ється на на́ших оча́х.
lines.source: That's how historians and guides tell it: the past seems to happen before our eyes.
lines.source_literal: So tell historians and guides: past as-if takes-place on our eyes.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: А для ме́не козаки́ означа́ють свобо́ду. Недарма́ в гі́мні ми співа́ємо, що ми «коза́цького ро́ду».
lines.source: And for me the Cossacks mean freedom. It's no accident that in the anthem we sing that we are 'of Cossack kin'.
lines.source_literal: And for me Cossacks mean freedom. Not-in-vain in anthem we sing, that we 'of-Cossack of-kin'.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: Різдво́, Вели́кдень, па́м’ять, іденти́чність and the other new words
grammar.explanation:
The new words of this unit follow the rules of the alphabet units and the unit on stress. The points below are the ones that are easy to miss.

'Різдво́' begins with a soft 'р', because 'р' is soft before the vowel letter 'і'. The 'з' and the 'д' are both voiced, so the cluster 'зд' is said as written, and 'в' before the vowel 'о' is [ʋ]: [rʲizdˈʋɔ]. The stress stays on the ending in the other forms: 'Різдва́', 'на Різдво́', 'з Різдво́м'. The word shares its root with 'наро́дження', birth: Christmas is the feast of the birth of Christ, 'Христо́с'.

'Вели́кдень' is a compound of 'вели́кий', great, and 'день', day: the Great Day. Where the two parts join, the adjective loses its ending '-ий', and 'к' meets 'д'. A voiceless consonant before a voiced one takes on its voice, as 'к' does before 'з' in 'вокза́л', so 'кд' is said [ɡd]: [ʋeˈlɪɡdenʲ]. In the other forms the 'е' of 'день' drops out, as it does in 'дня', and the linking vowel 'о' appears between the parts: 'Вели́кодня', 'з Вели́коднем'.

'Па́м’ять' has the apostrophe after 'м' before 'я', so the 'м' stays hard and a [j] is heard after it: [ˈpɑmjɑtʲ]. The final 'ть' is soft. In the instrumental the final consonant doubles before '-ю', as in 'сі́ллю': 'па́м’яттю'.

'Незале́жність' and 'іденти́чність' end in the suffix '-ість', which makes nouns of quality from adjectives: 'незале́жний', independent, gives 'незале́жність', independence. The 'і' of the suffix alternates with 'о', as in 'кіт', 'кота́'. 'О' appears before the ending '-і' ('незале́жності', 'іденти́чності'), and 'і' stays where there is no ending and before the instrumental '-ю' ('незале́жністю').

'Коза́к' and 'рушни́к' move the stress to the ending in the other forms, except the vocative 'коза́че': 'козака́', 'козаки́'; 'рушника́', 'рушники́'. 'Коза́к' also shows two changes of 'к'. Before the adjective suffix '-ськ-', 'к' and 'с' merge into 'ц': 'коза́цький'. Before the vocative ending '-е', 'к' becomes 'ч', as 'г' becomes 'ж' in 'дру́же': 'коза́че'.

'Гетьма́н' has a soft 'т', marked by the soft sign, before 'м'. 'Війна́' has 'й' before a consonant, and its plural moves the stress to the stem: 'ві́йни'. 'Пре́дки' is the plural of 'пре́док', whose 'о' drops when an ending is added, as in 'ри́нок', 'ри́нку'. In 'спа́дщина' the 'д' keeps its voice before 'щ' but moves toward 'щ', so it is said [d͡ʒ], the sound of 'дж': [ˈspɑd͡ʒʃt͡ʃɪnɑ].

'Вишива́нка', 'пи́санка' and 'коля́дка' are nouns in '-ка' made from 'вишива́ти', to embroider, 'писа́ти', to write, and 'коля́да', the old winter festival of carols. Their 'к' becomes 'ц' before '-і': 'у вишива́нці', 'на пи́санці'. 'Тради́ція' and 'істо́рія' end in '-ія': the consonant before 'і' is soft, and 'я' after the vowel 'і' is [jɑ]: [trɑˈdɪt͡sʲijɑ]. 'Звича́й' ends in 'й', so it takes the endings of a soft stem: 'звича́ю', 'звича́єм'.

The names of holidays, states and historical periods begin with a capital letter: 'Різдво́', 'Вели́кдень', 'День Незале́жності', 'Ки́ївська Русь', 'Гетьма́нщина'. The names of members of a group and titles do not: 'коза́к', 'гетьма́н', 'украї́нець'.

examples.source: Happy Easter, Mom!
Grandma lives on in our memory.
It's a question of identity.
Taras is reading about Cossack history.
Grandpa has an old embroidered towel.

grammar.title: The historical present: telling the past as if it were happening
grammar.explanation:
A story about the past can be told in the present tense, as if the events were happening before the reader's eyes. This is called the historical present. English uses it too, in timelines and documentaries ('In 1648, Khmelnytsky leads an uprising'). Ukrainian uses it widely in timelines, guided tours, documentaries and popular history, and a writer may also switch to it in the middle of a story in the past, at the moment the writer wants to make vivid. The dates and time words stay as they are; only the verbs change.

The present tense belongs to imperfective verbs only. A perfective verb has no present: its present-looking forms are its future, so 'очо́лить' means 'he will lead'. Every verb of a story in the historical present is therefore imperfective, even where the plain past would be perfective because it names one completed event. Each perfective of the past is replaced by its imperfective partner, often a secondary imperfective of the kind the unit on prefixes and aspect described:

- 'очо́лив', he led, becomes 'очо́лює', from 'очо́лювати', to lead, to head
- 'заснува́ли', they founded, becomes 'засно́вують', from 'засно́вувати'
- 'проголоси́ла', it proclaimed, with a feminine subject such as 'Верхо́вна Ра́да', becomes 'проголо́шує', from 'проголо́шувати', with 'с' changed to 'ш'
- 'прийня́в', he adopted, becomes 'прийма́є', from 'прийма́ти'
- 'став', he became, becomes 'стає́', from 'става́ти'
- 'ви́ник', it arose, becomes 'виника́є', from 'виника́ти'

In this use an imperfective present names one completed event, the job that a perfective does in the past. The verb no longer shows whether an event happened once or went on, so the context shows it: 'Хмельни́цький очо́лює повста́ння.' names one event, and a time word such as 'ча́сто' or 'ко́жного ро́ку' marks a repeated one. 'Повста́ння', an uprising, is a noun in '-ння' made from 'повста́ти', to rise up.

Inside a story in the historical present, an event that comes later can be told in the future, looking forward from the point the story has reached: 'Зго́дом він ста́не гетьма́ном.', 'Later he will become hetman.' Here a perfective future is correct, because it describes a result still to come from the story's point of view.

A text keeps one tense for its main line of events. It may begin in the past and move to the present at a decisive moment, but it does not move back and forth from sentence to sentence. In conversation, a question about the past still takes the past, as Sam's question in the museum does: 'Він очо́лив повста́ння в сімна́дцятому столі́тті, пра́вда?'

grammar.title: Centuries, dates and periods in historical writing
grammar.explanation:
The unit on numerals taught how to name a year ('у ти́сяча дев’ятсо́т дев’яно́сто пе́ршому ро́ці'), a full date and a century ('у двадця́тому столі́тті'). Historical writing adds ways to place an event inside a century and to name a stretch of time. In all of them the century or the year that something belongs to follows in the genitive, glossed 'of-'.

In print, centuries are written in Roman numerals and years in digits, and the reader supplies the ordinal and its case: XVII is read 'сімна́дцяте столі́ття', or 'у сімна́дцятому столі́тті' after 'у'. This course writes every number as words.

A part of a century or of a year is named by a noun in the locative, followed by the genitive:

- 'на поча́тку', at the beginning of, from 'поча́ток', beginning: 'на поча́тку двадця́того столі́ття'
- 'у середи́ні', in the middle of, from 'середи́на', middle: 'у середи́ні сімна́дцятого столі́ття'
- 'у пе́ршій полови́ні' and 'у дру́гій полови́ні', in the first and second half of: 'у дру́гій полови́ні дев’ятна́дцятого столі́ття'

The end is named by 'наприкінці́', at the end of, an adverb written as one word and built from 'кіне́ць', end. With the genitive it works like a preposition: 'наприкінці́ вісімна́дцятого столі́ття'.

A stretch of time has three patterns. 'З' and 'до' with the genitive mark its start and its end, and when both name centuries the noun is said once, at the end: 'з дев’я́того до трина́дцятого столі́ття', from the ninth to the thirteenth century. Two centuries named together take the noun in the plural: 'у п’ятна́дцятому й шістна́дцятому столі́ттях'. 'Протя́гом' with the genitive gives the length: 'протя́гом трьох столі́ть', for three centuries, with the genitive plural 'столі́ть' after the genitive 'трьох'.

Years before the birth of Christ are counted 'до на́шої е́ри', literally 'before our era', the Ukrainian equivalent of BC: 'у шо́стому столі́тті до на́шої е́ри'. 'На́шої е́ри', of our era, is added only where a reader could confuse the two. 'Пі́сля' and 'до' with the genitive place an event after or before a date: 'пі́сля ти́сяча дев’ятсо́т дев’яно́сто пе́ршого ро́ку'. As in a full date, only the last numeral of a year changes for case.

grammar.title: The four declensions of Ukrainian grammar
grammar.explanation:
Ukrainian grammar sorts nouns into four declensions, groups that share one set of endings. The Ukrainian term is 'відмі́на', from the same root as 'відмі́нок', case. The units on the cases taught the endings by gender and by stem; the four declensions gather the same endings into one system, the one that Ukrainian dictionaries and school grammars use. A noun's declension is decided by its nominative singular ending together with its gender:

- The first declension, 'пе́рша відмі́на': feminine, masculine and common-gender nouns in '-а' or '-я', such as 'держа́ва', 'пі́сня', 'тради́ція', and also 'Мико́ла' and 'коле́га'.
- The second declension, 'дру́га відмі́на': masculine nouns in a consonant or '-о', such as 'гетьма́н', 'звича́й', 'Вели́кдень' and 'та́то', and neuter nouns in '-о', '-е' or '-я', such as 'Різдво́', 'мо́ре' and 'життя́'.
- The third declension, 'тре́тя відмі́на': feminine nouns in a consonant, such as 'па́м’ять', 'незале́жність' and 'ніч', and the noun 'ма́ти', mother.
- The fourth declension, 'четве́рта відмі́на': neuter nouns in '-а' or '-я' that add a syllable to the stem in the other cases except the accusative, such as 'ім’я́', 'і́мені' and 'кошеня́', kitten, 'кошеня́ти'.

Inside the first and the second declensions the endings vary in a regular way with the last consonant of the stem: hard ('держа́ва', 'держа́вою'), soft ('пі́сня', 'пі́снею') or 'ж', 'ч', 'ш', 'щ' ('пло́ща', 'пло́щею'). Grammars call these the hard, the soft and the mixed groups.

Among masculine and feminine nouns, the first declension is defined by the ending, not by gender. 'Мико́ла' is a masculine noun: an adjective with it is masculine ('стари́й Мико́ла'), and the past tense agrees as for a man ('Мико́ла прийшо́в'). Its endings, though, are those of 'ма́ма': 'Мико́ли', 'Мико́лі', 'Мико́лу', 'Мико́лою'.

The third declension has endings of its own: '-і' in the genitive, the dative and the locative, the nominative form again in the accusative, except 'ма́тір' from 'ма́ти', and '-ю' in the instrumental. Before '-ю' a single final consonant doubles ('сі́ллю', 'па́м’яттю', 'Ру́ссю'), a final 'б', 'п', 'в', 'м', 'ф' or 'р' takes the apostrophe instead ('любо́в’ю', from 'любо́в', love, and 'ма́тір’ю'), and after two consonants nothing doubles ('незале́жністю', 'іденти́чністю'). 'Ма́ти' belongs here because its other forms are built on the stem 'ма́тер-', which ends in a consonant: 'ма́тері'.

The fourth declension is small. Nouns that add '-ат-' or '-ят-' name the young of people and animals: 'кошеня́', kitten, 'теля́', calf, 'дівча́', young girl. They decline 'кошеня́ти', 'кошеня́ті', 'кошеня́м', with the plural 'кошеня́та'. A few older nouns add '-ен-': 'ім’я́', 'і́мені', plural 'імена́', and 'пле́м’я', tribe, 'пле́мені', plural 'племена́'. In the genitive 'ім’я́' also has the short form 'ім’я́', and in the instrumental 'ім’я́м' beside 'і́менем'. 'Сім’я́', family, looks similar but is a feminine noun of the first declension: 'сім’ї́'.

Three kinds of noun stand outside the four declensions:

- nouns that decline like adjectives, such as 'ва́нна', 'знайо́мий' and 'лю́тий'
- nouns that never change, such as 'кафе́', 'метро́' and 'резюме́'
- plural-only nouns, such as 'гро́ші', 'две́рі' and 'кані́кули'

A dictionary gives the nominative and the genitive of a noun, and the two together show its declension: 'па́м’ять, па́м’яті' is third, and 'ім’я́, і́мені' is fourth.

grammar.title: Holiday greetings: 'з' with the instrumental and the genitive of wishing
grammar.explanation:
Holiday greetings are short, and most of them leave out a verb whose case the noun still shows. Two patterns cover nearly all of them.

The first is 'з' with the instrumental, short for 'Віта́ю вас з...', literally 'I-greet you with...'. 'Віта́ти', to greet or to congratulate ('віта́ю', 'віта́єш'), takes the person in the accusative and the occasion after 'з' in the instrumental: 'Віта́ю тебе́ з днем наро́дження!', 'Happy birthday!' Without the verb the greeting is 'З Різдво́м!', 'З Вели́коднем!' or 'З Нови́м ро́ком!', and 'Зі свя́том!' serves for any holiday, with 'зі' before 'св' by the euphony rule.

The second is the genitive of wishing, met in 'Смачно́го!' The verb 'бажа́ти', to wish, takes what is wished in the genitive ('Бажа́ю вам до́брого дня.'), and a greeting may keep only the genitive: 'Весе́лих свят!', 'Happy holidays!', literally 'of-merry of-holidays', from 'весе́лий', merry; 'Щасли́вого Різдва́!', 'Merry Christmas!', literally 'of-happy of-Christmas', from 'щасли́вий', happy; 'Смачно́ї куті́!', said at the Christmas Eve table.

Easter has a greeting of its own, which people exchange from Easter Sunday for forty days, in place of 'до́брий день': 'Христо́с воскре́с!', 'Christ is risen!', and the reply 'Воі́стину воскре́с!', 'He is risen indeed!' Both are fixed phrases:

- 'Воскре́с' is the masculine past of 'воскре́снути', to rise from the dead, without '-ну-' and without '-в', as 'встиг' is the past of 'всти́гнути'.
- 'Воі́стину' is a solemn church word for 'truly', from the old preposition 'во', in, and 'і́стину', the accusative of 'і́стина', truth. Its 'і' begins a new part of the word, so it is written 'і', not 'ї', and said [i] with no [j] before it: [vɔˈistɪnu].

These greetings go to anyone, with 'тебе́' or 'вас' as address requires: 'Віта́ю вас зі свя́том, па́ні Іри́но!'

Happy Easter!
I wish you happy holidays!

culture.title: Holidays, symbols and the days of the language
culture.text:
The Ukrainian calendar mixes church holidays, state holidays and days that celebrate the language and its symbols. The main ones are:

- 'Різдво́', Christmas: December 25, with Christmas Eve, 'Святве́чір', on December 24
- 'Вели́кдень', Easter: a Sunday in spring, on a date that changes every year
- 'День вишива́нки', Vyshyvanka Day: the third Thursday of May
- 'День Конститу́ції', Constitution Day: June 28
- 'День Незале́жності', Independence Day: August 24
- 'День украї́нської писе́мності та мо́ви', the Day of Ukrainian Writing and Language: November 9

Until 2023 most families celebrated Christmas on January 7, by the old church calendar. In 2023 the main churches of Ukraine moved their fixed holidays to a calendar that matches the one used in most of Europe, and the state holiday moved with them.

Vyshyvanka Day began in 2006 as the idea of a student at the university in Chernivtsi: on one day in May, people would wear an embroidered shirt to class or to work. It has since spread across the country and to Ukrainians abroad, and in many schools and offices most people wear one that day.

On November 9 Ukrainian radio holds a dictation for the whole country, 'радіодикта́нт', and thousands of people of every age write down a text read aloud on the air. 'Писе́мність' is the written tradition of a language. 'Та' in the name of the day is another word for 'and', common in writing and in names; it is spelled like 'та', the feminine of 'той'.

One Ukrainian song has traveled the world. 'Щедри́к' is a song for New Year's Eve of the kind called 'щедрі́вка', and the composer Mykola Leontovych arranged it for choir at the beginning of the twentieth century. A Ukrainian choir sang it on tour in America in the 1920s, and with English words it became the Christmas song known as 'Carol of the Bells'.

paragraphs.target: У дев’я́тому столі́тті навко́ло Ки́єва виника́є вели́ка держа́ва, Ки́ївська Русь. Ки́їв стає́ її́ столи́цею.

paragraphs.target: Наприкінці́ деся́того столі́ття князь Володи́мир прийма́є христия́нство. В одина́дцятому столі́тті його́ син Яросла́в Му́дрий буду́є в Ки́єві Софі́йський собо́р.

paragraphs.target: У двана́дцятому столі́тті Русь розпада́ється на окре́мі князі́вства, а в ти́сяча дві́сті сороко́вому ро́ці монго́ли руйну́ють Ки́їв.

paragraphs.target: У п’ятна́дцятому й шістна́дцятому столі́ттях на пі́вдні з’явля́ються козаки́. За поро́гами Дніпра́ вони́ засно́вують свою́ форте́цю, Запоро́зьку Січ.

paragraphs.target: У ти́сяча шістсо́т со́рок восьмо́му ро́ці гетьма́н Богда́н Хмельни́цький очо́лює повста́ння. Так виника́є коза́цька держа́ва, Гетьма́нщина.

paragraphs.source_literal: Christmas begins on-the-eve, on Holy-Evening. Family sits behind table, when on sky appears first star.

paragraphs.target: На стіл ста́влять двана́дцять страв без м’я́са. Пе́ршою їдя́ть кутю́, пшени́цю з ма́ком, ме́дом і горі́хами.
paragraphs.source: Twelve dishes without meat are put on the table. The first one eaten is kutia, wheat with poppy seeds, honey and nuts.
paragraphs.source_literal: On table they-put twelve of-dishes without meat. By-first they-eat kutia, wheat with poppy, honey and nuts.

paragraphs.target: У бага́тьох ха́тах у кутку́ стої́ть ді́дух, сніп пшени́ці. Він нага́дує про пре́дків, які́ ні́би святку́ють ра́зом із сім’є́ю.
paragraphs.source: In many homes a didukh, a sheaf of wheat, stands in the corner. It recalls the ancestors, who seem to celebrate together with the family.
paragraphs.source_literal: In many houses in corner stands didukh, sheaf of-wheat. It reminds about ancestors, who as-if celebrate together with family.

paragraphs.target: Пі́сля вече́рі співа́ють коля́дки. У за́хідних регіо́нах, особли́во на Гали́чині, коля́дники ще пока́зують верте́п, виста́ву про наро́дження Христа́.
paragraphs.source: After dinner people sing carols. In the western regions, especially in Halychyna, the region around Lviv, carolers also perform a vertep, a play about the birth of Christ.
paragraphs.source_literal: After dinner they-sing carols. In western regions, especially on Halychyna, carolers also show vertep, play about birth of-Christ.

paragraphs.target: Вели́кдень святку́ють навесні́. Пе́ред свя́том лю́ди фарбу́ють кра́шанки й розпи́сують пи́санки: візеру́нок малю́ють во́ском, а по́тім опуска́ють яйце́ у фа́рбу.
paragraphs.source: Easter is celebrated in spring. Before the holiday people dye eggs in one color and decorate pysanky: the pattern is drawn in wax, and then the egg is dipped in dye.
paragraphs.source_literal: Easter they-celebrate in-spring. Before holiday people dye dyed-eggs and paint decorated-eggs: pattern they-draw by-wax, and then lower egg into dye.

paragraphs.target: Пи́санки ко́жного регіо́ну ма́ють свої́ кольори́ й візеру́нки. Хто до́бре їх зна́є, той за візеру́нком мо́же сказа́ти, зві́дки пи́санка.
paragraphs.source: The pysanky of each region have their own colors and patterns. Someone who knows them well can tell from the pattern where a pysanka comes from.
paragraphs.source_literal: Decorated-eggs of-each of-region have own colors and patterns. Who well them knows, that-one by pattern can say, from-where decorated-egg.

paragraphs.target: Уве́чері в субо́ту або́ вра́нці в неді́лю лю́ди несу́ть до це́ркви ко́шики з па́скою, пи́санками, ковбасо́ю й си́ром, щоб їх посвяти́ти.
paragraphs.source: On Saturday evening or on Sunday morning people take baskets with paska, the Easter bread, and with pysanky, sausage and cheese to church to have them blessed.
paragraphs.source_literal: In-evening on Saturday or in-morning on Sunday people carry to church baskets with paska, decorated-eggs, sausage and cheese, so-that them to-bless.

paragraphs.target: Цього́ дня знайо́мі й незнайо́мі віта́ють одне́ о́дного слова́ми «Христо́с воскре́с!» і відповіда́ють «Воі́стину воскре́с!»
paragraphs.source: On this day friends and strangers greet each other with the words 'Christ is risen!' and answer 'He is risen indeed!'
paragraphs.source_literal: Of-this of-day acquaintances and strangers greet one another by-words 'Christ rose!' and answer 'In-truth rose!'

readings.title: The Ukrainian language in public life

paragraphs.target: У ти́сяча дев’ятсо́т дев’яно́сто шо́стому ро́ці Верхо́вна Ра́да ухвали́ла Конститу́цію Украї́ни. Вона́ назива́є украї́нську мо́ву держа́вною.
paragraphs.source: In 1996 the Verkhovna Rada adopted the Constitution of Ukraine. It names Ukrainian as the state language.
paragraphs.source_literal: In thousand nine-hundred ninety sixth year Supreme Council adopted Constitution of-Ukraine. It calls Ukrainian language by-state.

paragraphs.target: Украї́нською мо́вою працю́ють держа́вні устано́ви, суди́, шко́ли й університе́ти.
paragraphs.source: State institutions, courts, schools and universities work in Ukrainian.
paragraphs.source_literal: By-Ukrainian by-language work state institutions, courts, schools and universities.

paragraphs.target: У дві ти́сячі дев’ятна́дцятому ро́ці парла́мент ухвали́в зако́н про украї́нську мо́ву як держа́вну. Він визнача́є, де украї́нська обов’язко́ва.
paragraphs.source: In 2019 parliament adopted a law on Ukrainian as the state language. It sets out where Ukrainian is required.
paragraphs.source_literal: In two thousands nineteenth year parliament adopted law about Ukrainian language as state. It determines, where Ukrainian obligatory.

paragraphs.target: Відпові́дно до цього́ зако́ну, з дві ти́сячі два́дцять пе́ршого ро́ку магази́ни, кафе́ й ба́нки обслуго́вують клі́єнтів украї́нською. І́ншою мо́вою мо́жна говори́ти, якщо́ про це про́сить клі́єнт.
paragraphs.source: Under this law, since 2021 shops, cafés and banks have served customers in Ukrainian. Another language may be used if the customer asks for it.
paragraphs.source_literal: In-accordance with this law, from two thousands twenty of-first of-year shops, cafés and banks serve customers by-Ukrainian. By-other by-language possible to-speak, if about this asks customer.

paragraphs.target: Для бага́тьох украї́нців мо́ва ста́ла пита́нням іденти́чності, особли́во пі́сля поча́тку повномасшта́бної війни́ в дві ти́сячі два́дцять дру́гому ро́ці.
paragraphs.source: For many Ukrainians language has become a question of identity, especially since the start of the full-scale war in 2022.
paragraphs.source_literal: For many of-Ukrainians language became by-question of-identity, especially after beginning of-full-scale of-war in two thousands twenty second year.

paragraphs.target: Чима́ло люде́й, які́ вдо́ма говори́ли росі́йською, перейшли́ на украї́нську. Опитува́ння пока́зують, що украї́нською тепе́р гово́рить бі́льше люде́й, ніж до війни́.
paragraphs.source: Many people who spoke Russian at home have switched to Ukrainian. Surveys show that more people now speak Ukrainian than before the war.
paragraphs.source_literal: Quite-many of-people, who at-home spoke by-Russian, crossed to Ukrainian. Surveys show, that by-Ukrainian now speaks more of-people, than before war.

questions.prompt: What does the Constitution of 1996 say about Ukrainian?
choices: It names Ukrainian as the state language
It makes Ukrainian one of two state languages
questions.explanation: 'Вона́ назива́є украї́нську мо́ву держа́вною': the Constitution names Ukrainian as the state language.

questions.prompt: Under the law of 2019, how must shops, cafés and banks serve customers?
choices: In any language the staff prefer
In Ukrainian, unless the customer asks for another language
Only in Ukrainian, whatever the customer asks
questions.explanation: 'І́ншою мо́вою мо́жна говори́ти, якщо́ про це про́сить клі́єнт.' Ukrainian is the default, and another language is possible at the customer's request.

questions.prompt: What do surveys show since the start of the full-scale war?
choices: Fewer people speak Ukrainian than before
More people speak Ukrainian than before the war
questions.explanation: 'Украї́нською тепе́р гово́рить бі́льше люде́й, ніж до війни́.' Many who spoke Russian at home have switched to Ukrainian.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian with the English
Match the traditions with their English names

exercises.audio_target: Бабу́ся бага́то розповіда́ла нам про війну́.
choices: Grandma told us a lot about Christmas.
Grandma told us a lot about the war.
Grandma wrote to us a lot about the war.
This is a very old song.
This is a very old towel.
This is a very old custom.

exercises.audio_target: Це було́ на поча́тку двадця́того столі́ття.
choices: That was at the end of the twentieth century.
That was at the beginning of the twentieth century.
That was at the beginning of the twenty-first century.

exercises.prompt: Which word names a custom shared by a community, rather than one person's habit?
exercises.explanation: 'Звича́й' is a custom of a community; 'зви́чка' is one person's habit, and 'па́м’ять' is memory.
'Пре́дки' is the plural of 'пре́док', an ancestor; 'пре́дка' is its genitive singular.

exercises.prompt: What does 'Вели́кдень' say word for word?
exercises.explanation: It is a compound of 'вели́кий', great, and 'день', day. 'Святве́чір', Christmas Eve, is the holy evening.

exercises.prompt: Why does a history text say 'Хмельни́цький очо́лює повста́ння' and not 'Хмельни́цький очо́лить повста́ння'?
choices: 'Очо́лить' is a perfective future and would mean 'will lead'
exercises.explanation: The historical present needs a present form, and only imperfective verbs have one. 'Очо́лить' is the future of the perfective 'очо́лити'.

exercises.prompt: A story told in the historical present says: 'Зго́дом він ста́не гетьма́ном.' What does this tell the reader?
choices: That he was a hetman before the story began
That later in the story he becomes hetman
That he wants to become hetman
exercises.explanation: Inside a story in the historical present, a perfective future looks forward from the point the story has reached.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase means 'at the end of the eighteenth century'?
exercises.explanation: 'Наприкінці́' with the genitive is at the end of; 'на поча́тку' is at the beginning of and 'у середи́ні' in the middle of.
A masculine or feminine noun in '-а' or '-я' belongs to the first declension whatever its gender. 'Мико́ла' is masculine in agreement, but it declines like 'ма́ма'.

exercises.prompt: Which noun belongs to the fourth declension?
exercises.explanation: 'Ім’я́' adds '-ен-' in its other forms: 'і́мені'. 'Сім’я́' and 'земля́' are feminine nouns of the first declension.

exercises.prompt: Why is the instrumental of 'па́м’ять' 'па́м’яттю', but that of 'незале́жність' 'незале́жністю'?
choices: A single final consonant doubles before '-ю', and after two consonants nothing doubles
exercises.explanation: Both are feminine nouns of the third declension. 'Па́м’ять' ends in one consonant, 'ть', which doubles; 'незале́жність' ends in two, 'сть'.
The Easter reply is 'Воі́стину воскре́с!', 'He is risen indeed!' The other two are Christmas greetings.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'Смачно́ї куті́!' in the genitive?
choices: It is a wish, and 'бажа́ти', to wish, takes the genitive
exercises.explanation: The greeting keeps only the genitive of 'Бажа́ю смачно́ї куті́!', as 'Смачно́го!' does.
A voiceless consonant before a voiced one takes on its voice, as in 'вокза́л', so 'к' before 'д' is said [ɡ].

exercises.prompt: In the first dialogue, how old is the embroidered towel on the wall?
exercises.explanation: 'Цьому́ рушнику́ вже сто ро́ків.' Halyna's grandmother embroidered it.

exercises.prompt: In the second dialogue, why does the guide tell the Cossacks' story in the present tense?
choices: He does not know the past forms
The exhibition is about Cossacks of today
The past then seems to happen before the listeners' eyes
exercises.explanation: 'Мину́ле ні́би відбува́ється на на́ших оча́х.' Sam, asking a question, uses the past: 'Він очо́лив повста́ння'.

exercises.hint_source: We celebrated Independence Day in Kyiv.
exercises.explanation: The name of the day is 'День Незале́жності', with the genitive of 'незале́жність', where the 'і' of '-ість' becomes 'о'. The capital letter is written in the name.

exercises.hint_source: In the evening we sang carols.
exercises.explanation: 'Коля́дки', the plural of 'коля́дка', names things, not people or animals, so its accusative is the same as its nominative.

exercises.hint_source: Sam came to the celebration in an embroidered shirt.
exercises.explanation: 'У' with the locative: 'вишива́нка' becomes 'у вишива́нці', with 'к' changed to 'ц' before '-і'.

exercises.hint_source: This film is about the war.
exercises.explanation: 'Про' takes the accusative, and 'війна́' becomes 'війну́'.

exercises.prompt_target: У ти́сяча дев’ятсо́т дев’яно́сто шо́стому ро́ці Украї́на ___ Конститу́цію.
exercises.explanation: In the historical present a single completed event takes the imperfective present: 'прийма́є' from 'прийма́ти', or 'ухва́лює' from 'ухва́лювати'. The perfectives 'прийня́ти' and 'ухвали́ти' have no present.

exercises.prompt_target: У дев’я́тому столі́тті Ки́їв ___ столи́цею Ру́сі.
exercises.hint_source: In the ninth century Kyiv becomes the capital of Rus.
exercises.explanation: 'Става́ти', the imperfective of 'ста́ти', gives the historical present 'стає́'; 'ста́не' would mean 'will become'.

exercises.prompt_target: Цей собо́р збудува́ли в ___ полови́ні одина́дцятого столі́ття.
exercises.hint_source: This cathedral was built in the first half of the eleventh century.
exercises.explanation: 'У пе́ршій полови́ні' is a locative, and the ordinal agrees with the feminine 'полови́на': 'пе́ршій'. The century follows in the genitive.

exercises.hint_source: I don't remember this hetman's name.
exercises.explanation: After a negated verb the object may be in the genitive, 'і́мені', with the '-ен-' of the fourth declension, or in the accusative, 'ім’я́'.
'Віта́ти з' takes the instrumental: 'свя́то' becomes 'свя́том', and 'з' becomes 'зі' before 'св'.

exercises.prompt_source: The children sang carols under the windows.
The hetman leads a Cossack uprising.

exercises.hint_source: This is an old custom of our ancestors.
We remember the history of our state.
Merry Christmas and Happy New Year!

exercises.explanation: 'Тради́ція' is feminine, so the adjective is 'стара́'. 'Це' points, and no word for 'is' is needed.
'Святкува́ти' changes '-ува-' to '-у-' in the present: 'святку́ємо'. 'Різдво́' is neuter, so its accusative is the same as its nominative.
'Пам’ята́ти' takes the accusative, 'війну́', directly or after 'про'.
'З' with the instrumental 'Вели́коднем', or the genitive of wishing, 'Вели́кодня'. In both, the 'е' of 'день' drops and the linking 'о' appears.
